questions.q: On a slow network, Rebecca taps "Send" twice and the money is deducted twice. Which fix goes to the root of the problem?
questions.hint: Would the fix still work if the page is refreshed, or the mobile app retries by itself?

options.text: Disable the button after the first click
options.why: Good practice, but it doesn't stop a refresh, a second tab or an auto-retry. The server still can't tell two requests apart.

options.text: The client sends an idempotency key, and the server recognizes it and returns the earlier reply for the same key
options.why: However the request arrives twice, the server knows it is the same job and does it only once.

options.text: Raise the server timeout to 60 seconds
options.why: If the reply is lost on the way, no timeout will tell the client whether the work was done.

options.text: Block a second transfer of the same amount within a minute
options.why: It is guesswork: someone who really wants to send the same amount twice gets blocked, and a retry after a minute slips through.

questions.q: What problems does the guard code below have?
questions.hint: Look at two places: the gap between checking and writing, and the gap between the work and saving the key.

options.text: If two requests with the same key arrive together, both see "no key" and both do the work
options.why: Checking (SELECT) and writing (INSERT) are separate steps, and the second request slips into the gap. The fix is a direct INSERT backed by a unique constraint.

options.text: If it crashes after the work but before the key is saved, a retry does the whole job again
options.why: The work and the key are committed in different transactions. Unless both are in one transaction, this gap is always there.

options.text: findOneBy() is slow; using find() would fix it
options.why: Speed isn't the problem. However fast the lookup, the gap between checking and writing remains.

options.text: The key should have been an auto-increment number rather than a UUID
options.why: The client makes the key, and it must be able to produce a unique value without the server's help. That is exactly why UUIDs are used.

questions.q: A request for $50 arrives with an idempotency key, and a while later a request for $500 arrives with the same key. What should the server do?
questions.hint: What does a bank do when a check number comes back with a different amount?

options.text: Return the stored reply from the $50 request
options.why: The client would think $500 went through when only $50 did. The mistake would be hidden.

options.text: Treat it as a new request and send $500
options.why: Then the key means nothing: two different transfers happened under one key.

options.text: Turn it away with 422 because the fingerprint doesn't match
options.why: The same key with a different request means a bug in the client's code. Only a clear error gets it noticed.

options.text: Quietly ignore the request and return 200
options.why: 200 means "the work was done". Returning 200 without doing anything is lying to the client.

questions.q: The Vue app sends a transfer request and gets no reply after 10 seconds (a timeout). What should the client do next?
questions.hint: Does the client know right now whether the money moved?

options.text: Make a new key and send again
options.why: If the first request succeeded, a request with a new key will deduct the money a second time.

options.text: Send again with the same key
options.why: If the first one went through, the stored reply comes back; if not, it will now happen once. Safe either way.

options.text: Show "failed" and stop
options.why: A timeout doesn't mean failure, it means "we don't know". The money may have gone, and the user is being told something false.

options.text: Assume it succeeded and move to the next page
options.why: The request may never have reached the server. Showing success without knowing is just as wrong.

questions.q: Which of these writes are safe to run twice even without an idempotency key?
questions.hint: Which are "set this value" writes, and which are "add another one" writes?

options.text: PUT /users/7: set the whole profile to new values
options.why: Setting the same values twice leaves the profile the same.

options.text: UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = 9
options.why: If the status is already paid, setting it to paid again changes nothing.

options.text: POST /transfers: create a new transfer
options.why: Each run creates a new transfer; arriving twice sends the money twice.

options.text: UPDATE wallet SET balance = balance + 100
options.why: Each run adds another 100. This is an "increase" write.

options.text: DELETE /cart/items/5
options.why: Once the item is gone, deleting it again leaves the same state (at worst you get a 404).

questions.q: In IdempotencyGuard, the key row, the money transfer and the stored reply share one transaction. An exception is thrown halfway through sending the money. What does a retry with the same key get?
questions.hint: What happens to the key row when the transaction rolls back?

options.text: A stored "success" reply, even though no money moved
options.why: Everything rolled back before any reply was stored; there is no stored reply.

options.text: A permanent "key already used" error
options.why: That would happen if the key had been committed first in a separate transaction. Here the key rolled back too.

options.text: The whole job runs again from scratch, because the key row was rolled back too
options.why: That is the benefit of one transaction: if the work doesn't happen, the key doesn't stay either, so the retry starts from a clean state.

questions.q: What is the risk if the idempotency table has no scope (such as a user id) and only a unique constraint on the key?
questions.hint: What happens if two different users send the same key?

options.text: If one user's key collides with another's, that person could receive the other's stored reply
options.why: The key then lives in one namespace shared by everyone. If someone knows another's key, or a bug makes them collide, details of another person's transfer leak.

options.text: The database won't be able to create the unique index at all
options.why: A unique index on a single column is perfectly possible; the problem is security, not a technical limit.

options.text: The client can no longer generate UUIDs
options.why: Making the UUID is entirely the client's job; it has nothing to do with how the server's table is built.

questions.q: Ryan's webhook handler marks the order paid just because the body says `status: paid`, with no signature check. What is the biggest risk?
questions.hint: Who can find out what the URL is?

options.text: Anyone can POST a fake call and get an order marked paid with no money
options.why: The URL is open, and the handler doesn't check who the sender is. So even fake news becomes the truth.

options.text: The gateway's server will slow down
options.why: Without verification the handler actually runs faster. The problem is trust, not speed.

options.text: Parsing the JSON will take longer
options.why: The time spent parsing has nothing to do with security.

options.text: The same order will be saved twice in the database
options.why: That is a different problem (duplicates). The main risk here is a fake sender.

questions.q: What is wrong with the signature check in the code below?
questions.hint: What exactly is being hashed, and how is the comparison done?

options.text: It hashes the re-encoded array, not the raw body; if the bytes differ, the seal won't match
options.why: You must hash exactly the bytes the gateway sealed. Decoding and re-encoding can change whitespace or key order.

options.text: It compares with `==` instead of hash_equals
options.why: A plain comparison opens the door to timing attacks. Always use hash_equals to check a seal.

options.text: sha256 is far too weak; sha1 should be used
options.why: The other way around: sha256 is fine, and sha1 is old and weak.

options.text: You needn't think about timestamps, because the HMAC is enough
options.why: Without a timestamp, a genuine sealed request can be sent again later (a replay). So the timestamp should be part of the seal too.

questions.q: Which approach is the right way to handle slow work at a webhook endpoint?
questions.hint: How long does the gateway wait? Who retries when the work fails?

options.text: Verify the seal, store the event, dispatch to Messenger, and return 200 straight away
options.why: The gateway gets a quick reply, and the slow work runs in a worker, which has its own retries.

options.text: Finish all the work in the controller, then return 200
options.why: If it is slow, the gateway times out and resends the same event, so duplicates multiply.

options.text: Return 200 before the work is done, without storing anything
options.why: If the server then crashes, the event is lost for good, and the gateway thinks the news was delivered.

options.text: Return 500 for every event so the gateway keeps resending
options.why: Every event then goes into the retry queue, and in the end the gateway may disable the endpoint altogether.

questions.q: A webhook delivers `payment.succeeded` first, then an older `payment.pending`. The handler does `status = event.status`. What happens?
questions.hint: Do retries and networks keep the order intact?

options.text: The payment goes from succeeded back to pending, and the customer paid but finds the order stuck
options.why: The old news arrived later and wiped out the newer state. If only forward transitions were valid in a state machine, this would be rejected.

options.text: The gateway guarantees order, so this never happens
options.why: Most gateways give no ordering guarantee, especially when retrying.

options.text: The handler will ignore the second event automatically
options.why: Nothing like that exists: the code does what it says (set the status).

questions.q: Which of these keep a webhook handler safe from duplicate events?
questions.hint: Can the handler tell whether this is the first or the second arrival?

options.text: A unique constraint on event_id in the webhook_event table
options.why: The same event arriving again creates no new row, so there is a basis for spotting the duplicate.

options.text: `UPDATE ... SET processed_at = now() WHERE event_id = ? AND processed_at IS NULL`, returning when 0 rows change
options.why: When two come at once, the database gives only one of them 1 row. The other gets 0 and skips the work.

options.text: SELECT first to see whether the event exists, then INSERT
options.why: If two requests arrive together, both will see "not there". There is a gap between checking and writing.

options.text: Tell the gateway never to retry
options.why: Turn off retries and an event is lost for good on a 500 or a timeout. Handling duplicates is your side's job.

questions.q: The database is down at your webhook endpoint, so the event can't be stored. Which reply should you give?
questions.hint: When does the gateway send again?

options.text: 200, and fix it later
options.why: The gateway will assume the news was delivered and never send it again. The event is lost for good.

options.text: 401, because something is wrong
options.why: 401 means a wrong seal. Here the seal is fine; the fault is on your server.

options.text: 500, so the gateway sends it again on its retry schedule
options.why: If the event isn't stored, you can't reply 2xx. A 5xx means "I couldn't take it, try again".

questions.q: The handler claimed a `payment.succeeded` event, but no payment has that gateway id yet: the reply carrying the id has not been saved. What should it do?
questions.hint: Will the gateway ever send this event again?

options.text: Throw so the claim rolls back and Messenger retries later
options.why: The payment is behind the event. Once the id is saved, the retry finds it, applies `succeed` and the payment moves on.

options.text: Return quietly; the event is already marked processed
options.why: That throws the event away. The gateway will not resend it, so the payment stays in `pending` forever.

options.text: Create a new payment row from the event's data and mark it succeeded
options.why: The event is not the record of what you sold, and the original row would turn up later as a duplicate payment.

options.text: Return 500 from the controller so the gateway sends it again
options.why: The controller already stored the event and replied 200. The decision is made later, in the worker.

questions.q: In Ryan's payments table the status is a plain `VARCHAR`, and code in many places calls `setStatus()` directly. Which problem is the most likely?
questions.hint: If an old event arrives late, what will stop it?

options.text: A stale event will arrive and turn a succeeded payment back into pending
options.why: The status accepts any value, and the rule "no going backwards" lives nowhere.

options.text: The database won't be able to store a `VARCHAR`
options.why: VARCHAR works fine; the problem is the rules, not the type.

options.text: Payments can't be created at all
options.why: Creating them works fine; what you can't do is stop wrong changes.

options.text: Updating the status column will be very slow
options.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

questions.q: In the config below, where does the `refund` transition go from and to? And which states are terminal?
questions.hint: What do you call a state that never appears in a `from:`?

options.text: refund: succeeded → refunded; failed and refunded are terminal
options.why: failed and refunded appear in no transition's from, so there is no way out of them.

options.text: refund: failed → refunded; only created is terminal
options.why: created has submit, and refund's from is succeeded.

options.text: refund: pending → refunded; only succeeded is terminal
options.why: There is no refund from pending; and refund leaves succeeded, so it isn't terminal.

options.text: No state is terminal; every state has some way out
options.why: No arrow leaves failed or refunded.

questions.q: A payment is in the pending state. According to the diagram, which transitions are directly legal from here?
questions.hint: Count the arrows leaving pending.

options.text: succeed
options.why: pending → succeeded, when the gateway reports the money arrived.

options.text: fail
options.why: pending → failed, when the gateway reports a failure.

options.text: refund
options.why: refund runs only from succeeded; there is nothing to give back before the money arrives.

options.text: submit
options.why: submit takes created to pending. The payment is already in pending.

questions.q: In Symfony a payment should be in exactly one state at a time, with no parallel steps. Which config is right?
questions.hint: Can one thing be in two places at once?

options.text: `type: workflow`, because it is the default and works for everything
options.why: In the workflow type a thing can be in several places at once; we don't want that for a payment.

options.text: `type: state_machine`, `marking_store: {type: method, property: status}`
options.why: state_machine keeps only one place at a time, and the method marking store keeps the value in the entity's status property.

options.text: No config needed; just write `if ($status === ...)` in the code
options.why: Scattered ifs bring back the old problem: the rules aren't in one place, and mistakes aren't stopped.

questions.q: Two workers run the `succeed` and `fail` transitions on the same pending payment at the same time. Is the code below safe?
questions.hint: What happens if another worker slips in between the read and the write?

options.text: Not safe: both can see pending, and the last flush wins
options.why: can() only looks at its own in-memory object. It can't know what another worker did in the database.

options.text: Safe, because there is a can()
options.why: can() sees a snapshot from the moment of reading. If another worker changes it in the gap, it has no idea.

options.text: Safe, because Doctrine automatically locks the row
options.why: By default find() takes no lock. You have to ask for a LockMode or a version column separately.

options.text: Safe, because the state machine opens a transaction itself
options.why: The Workflow component never touches the database; transactions and locks are your job.

questions.q: Which approaches make the race between two transitions on the same payment safe?
questions.hint: How does the database make sure whoever arrives first wins?

options.text: Read the row with `LockMode::PESSIMISTIC_WRITE` inside a transaction, then can()/apply()
options.why: The second worker waits, then sees the new status.

options.text: A `#[ORM\Version]` column on the entity, catching the conflict exception and retrying
options.why: The version is checked at write time; the one that arrives later fails.

options.text: Adding a `sleep(1)` between the two workers
options.why: It relies on timing: it will work sometimes and fail other times. That doesn't solve a race.

options.text: Calling can() twice
options.why: Even called twice, both calls see the same stale snapshot.

questions.q: A gateway call times out after 5 seconds. What is the app's correct next step?
questions.hint: What does a timeout prove: that the work didn't happen, or that no reply came?

options.text: Mark the payment failed and tell the customer to try again
options.why: The money may already have been taken. If the customer tries again, it may be taken a second time.

options.text: Mark the payment succeeded and ship the order
options.why: The goods would go out even if the money was never taken. A timeout is not proof of success.

options.text: Keep the payment pending and ask the gateway later
options.why: Pending is the right home for an unknown state. The real result then comes from a status query or a webhook.

options.text: Immediately send the same request again with a new key
options.why: A new key means new work. If the first one succeeded, the money will be taken twice.

questions.q: What is wrong with the code below?
questions.hint: When is the key made? What state is set on a timeout? And is there a timeout option?

options.text: A new key every time, so on a retry the gateway will take the money again
options.why: The key must be tied to the payment, not to the attempt.

options.text: Every exception sets failed, so a timeout counts as a failure too
options.why: The outcome of a timeout is unknown. If you mark it failed, money that was taken is never caught.

options.text: There is no `timeout` option, so the call could hang indefinitely
options.why: Every outside call should have a timeout, otherwise your app's worker gets stuck.

options.text: You shouldn't POST with HttpClient at all
options.why: HttpClient is the right tool; the trouble is in how the key, exceptions and timeout are handled.

questions.q: The gateway returns 402 (card declined) on one call and 503 on another. What state do the two payments end up in?
questions.hint: 4xx versus 5xx: which is a final "no", and which is "I can't right now"?

options.text: Both failed
options.why: 503 means the gateway can't respond right now; you can't say whether the money was taken.

options.text: Both pending
options.why: 402 is a clear rejection, so there is no reason to keep it pending.

options.text: 402 → failed, 503 → pending
options.why: A clear rejection is final; a 5xx is unknown.

options.text: 402 → pending, 503 → failed
options.why: Exactly backwards: 402 is final, 503 is unknown.

questions.q: Ryan decides that if a payment is still pending after 1 hour, the app will mark it "failed" itself, without waiting for a webhook or a query. What is the problem?
questions.hint: Does the money go back just because time has passed?

options.text: Time passing doesn't prove the money wasn't taken. It may still be taken at the gateway
options.why: The truth is with the gateway. You learn the result by asking the gateway, not from a timer.

options.text: One hour is too short; 24 hours would be safe
options.why: Whatever the time, a guess is a guess. You can't call it failed without asking the gateway.

options.text: There is no problem; one hour is enough
options.why: If the gateway's ledger later says "succeeded", the customer has been charged while the order is canceled.

questions.q: Which measures help stop a payment staying pending forever?
questions.hint: If one path fails, what do the others do?

options.text: A regular sweeper that picks up pending payments older than 15 minutes and queries them again
options.why: If a webhook or an earlier query is lost, this sweeper is the last safety net.

options.text: Scheduling a CheckPaymentStatus message 30 seconds after the charge call
options.why: With a check on time, most payments are settled quickly.

options.text: Relying on the webhook alone
options.why: A webhook can be lost or arrive very late; on its own it is not enough.

options.text: Telling the customer to phone the bank themselves
options.why: The problem is in our system; pushing it onto the customer is no solution.

questions.q: A status query makes the gateway say "I don't recognize this reference". What is the safest next step?
questions.hint: When you send the charge again, which does the gateway go by: the old key or a new one?

options.text: Make a new key and send the charge again
options.why: If the earlier call arrives late, the new key means the work happens twice.

options.text: Mark the payment succeeded
options.why: The gateway doesn't recognize it at all, so the money was not taken. Calling it a success is wrong.

options.text: Send the charge again with the same earlier idempotency key
options.why: If the call never arrived, the work now happens once; if it did, the gateway returns the earlier result.
